topics.title: 15.1 Addition
topics.summary: addq source, destination adds 64-bit operands and stores the low 64 bits in the destination. It updates condition flags, including carry and signed overflow indicators. A register-memory form also performs the relevant memory access. The low-bit addition result can serve either signed or unsigned interpretation. Carry indicates unsigned overflow beyond the width; overflow indicates that the signed result cannot be represented. These flags answer different questions. An assembly routine exposing checked arithmetic must return or branch on the appropriate condition rather than assuming the caller can inspect flags after an ordinary C call.

topics.title: 15.2 Subtraction
topics.summary: subq source, destination computes destination minus source. This operand order is easy to reverse when switching between AT&T and Intel syntax. The result updates flags used by both arithmetic and comparisons. Subtraction underlies cmp , which computes flags without retaining the result. For unsigned order, carry-related conditions describe borrow behavior. For signed order, the sign and overflow relationship matters. A raw negative-looking high bit is not enough to establish the result of a signed comparison after overflow-sensitive subtraction.

topics.title: 15.3 Multiplication
topics.summary: The imul family supports signed multiplication in several forms. Two-operand forms retain the low-width result, while one-operand forms can produce a double-width result using implicit registers. Unsigned mul also uses implicit accumulator registers for full-width products. The low w bits of a product are the same under signed and unsigned modular interpretations of the input patterns. The high half and overflow interpretation differ. A compiler can therefore use a signed-named multiply instruction for some unsigned low-result calculations. Read the instruction’s actual result width and use, not only its mnemonic’s historical label.

topics.title: 15.4 Division
topics.summary: For 64-bit signed idivq , the dividend is in %rdx:%rax , the divisor is the explicit operand, the quotient is returned in %rax , and the remainder in %rdx . cqto sign-extends %rax into %rdx when dividing an ordinary signed 64-bit dividend. The instruction faults for a zero divisor or an unrepresentable quotient. It does not return an ordinary error code. Validate the input contract before executing it when building a checked interface. For unsigned divq of a 64-bit value, a zero high half is typically prepared, but only when that matches the intended double-width dividend.

topics.title: 15.5 Increment/decrement
topics.summary: inc and dec add or subtract one. They update several arithmetic flags but do not update the carry flag. This difference can matter when a later instruction consumes carry from an earlier operation. A compiler may choose add $1 or sub $1 instead, depending on code size, dependencies, and target tuning. Do not use instruction spelling as the sole measure of efficiency. The surrounding flag dependencies and pipeline behavior can be more important than the apparent simplicity of “increment.”

topics.title: 15.8 XOR
topics.summary: xor toggles differing bits. A common zeroing idiom is xorl %eax, %eax , which produces a full zero in %rax because a 32-bit register write clears the high half. It also changes flags, so it cannot be inserted between a comparison and a branch without considering that dependency. A zeroing idiom may be recognized specially by the microarchitecture, but its correctness follows from the architectural XOR result. A programmer should first establish that zero is the required value and that flag changes are harmless. Performance tuning follows only after those conditions are satisfied.

topics.title: 15.9 Shifts
topics.summary: Logical shifts move bits and fill with zeros; arithmetic right shift replicates the sign bit. In AT&T syntax, shl or sal names left shift, shr logical right shift, and sar arithmetic right shift. Traditional variable counts use %cl . x86 masks shift counts according to operand width, but C and C++ source shifts with out-of-range counts are not thereby made valid. Hardware behavior is not a substitute for language preconditions. Likewise, arithmetic right shift of a negative value rounds differently from signed division by a positive power of two when the value is not evenly divisible. [ R3 , R36 ]

topics.title: Worked example — Signed division with explicit preparation
topics.summary: The requirement is to divide -29 by 6. The mathematical quotient truncated toward zero is -4, and the remainder is -5 because -29 = (-4)*6 + (-5) . Companion listing: ch15/divide.S Companion listing: ch15/main.c Before idivq , %rax holds the two’s-complement pattern for -29 and %rdx is all ones. This pair represents the sign-extended dividend. Afterward %rax is -4 and %rdx is -5. Clearing %rdx instead would describe a large positive double-width number, not -29, and could cause a quotient-overflow fault.
